fācundĭa , ae, f. facundus,
I.eloquence, fluency (like facundus, not freq. till after the Aug. period; “not in Cic., Caes., or Liv.): hic actor tantum poterit a facundia,” Ter. Heaut. prol. 13 : “facundia Graecos, gloria belli Gallos ante Romanos fuisse,” Sall. C. 53, 3 ; so, “Graeca,” id. J. 63, 3 : “Graeca Latinaque,” Suet. Calig. 20 ; cf. Quint. 12, 10, 27; Plin. 7, 30, 31, § 117: alere facundiam, Quint. prooem. § 23; Hor. C. 4, 7, 21; Quint. 2, 16, 10; 8, 1, 3; 10, 1, 80 et saep.; Tac. A. 11, 6; Gell. 11, 13, 10; 18, 5, 1; 19, 9, 7 al.—In plur., Gell. 3, 17, 1.—Transf., of a person, Ov. P. 1, 2, 69.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
